result:
There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just before rain. The birds stop arguing. Leaves turn their pale undersides toward the sky. Somewhere, a person standing at a kitchen sink pauses without knowing why. The world seems to be listening for a name it cannot quite remember anymore.

I like to imagine that rain is not weather but correspondence. Each drop carries a small message from somewhere else: a mountain stream, a steaming cup, the breath of an animal sleeping beneath a tree. Nothing in the world stays entirely separate. Even distance is sometimes only a temporary arrangement.

When the first drops land, they make dark coins on the pavement. Then the coins overlap, and the pavement becomes a mirror that refuses to hold still. Streetlights stretch into trembling ribbons. Ordinary buildings acquire secret depths. A bus goes by carrying twenty private stories through one shared silver afternoon.

We spend so much time trying to become remarkable that we overlook the strange privilege of being here at all. To feel cold water slip beneath a collar. To smell dust becoming earth again. To hear someone laugh under an umbrella that is clearly too small for both of them anyway.

Eventually, the clouds move on. Gutters finish their hurried speeches. A sparrow tests the air, then another answers. People step outside as though returning from a long voyage. Nothing important has happened, perhaps. Yet everything has been touched, and for a little while the familiar world looks newly worth noticing.
